title: Intro to Docker
summary: Containers: why they exist, how they compare to virtual machines, how a Dockerfile becomes an image and an image becomes a container, and how to inspect and clean them up. The step-by-step arrives when the lecture is published.
goal: Write a small Dockerfile, build it into an image, run it as a throwaway container, and clean up after yourself.

steps.title: Read the two Docker lessons
steps.detail: Skim Introduction to Docker and Leveraging Docker on the curriculum site. Watch for: image vs container, the Dockerfile instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD), and --rm.
steps.doneWhen: You can explain the difference between an image and a container.

steps.title: Check Docker runs on your Mac
steps.detail: Docker is already installed. Open Docker Desktop first, then run a one-off test container. --rm deletes the container when it exits.
steps.code:
docker --version
docker run --rm hello-world
docker ps -a
steps.doneWhen: You see "Hello from Docker!", and docker ps -a lists no leftover hello-world container.

steps.title: Skim the Docker Fundamentals README
steps.detail: The curriculum's assignment is Docker Fundamentals: four small tasks, one folder each (task-1-hello on alpine, a file read, env vars, a script), all run as disposable one-off containers. Read it now; wait for Slack before forking.
steps.doneWhen: You know the four tasks and what "end-state" each one asks for.

concepts.meaning: A running, isolated copy of an app and everything it needs.
The read-only template a container starts from, built from a Dockerfile.
A text recipe: start FROM a base image, COPY files, RUN setup, set the CMD to run.
A VM fakes a whole computer; a container shares your OS kernel, so it's much lighter and faster.
A docker run flag that deletes the container as soon as it exits.
